Although values are extracted by pyparsing from `valid_word` (which excludes some special characters), the exclusion set (`'=><(){}[]^"~*?:\/.&|'`) does not block characters such as spaces, semicolons, hyphens, or other SQL-significant characters that can appear in `printables`. A crafted query like `"; DROP TABLE alerts; --:value` could inject SQL through the field name slot. This is a newly introduced code path (the PR adds `to_sql` where previously `__repr__` was used), so the exposure is new. findings.explanation: The PR changes `qvars` initialization from `dict()` to `dict(parsed_vars)`, where `parsed_vars` is the `params` dict returned directly by `QueryParser.parse()` (postgres/queryparser.py line 286-289). This `params` dict is populated by user-supplied query string values (the `q=` parameter). After this change, `qvars` is seeded with attacker-controlled key-value pairs before the customer authorization filter is applied. At lines 161-163, the customer restriction is added: `qvars['customers'] = customers`. However, if a user crafts a `q=` query that causes `parsed_vars` to contain a key named `customers`, the later assignment at line 163 will overwrite it — but if the order were reversed, or if the SQL template uses a `parsed_vars`-originated `customers` binding that shadows the authorization value in a psycopg2 binding context, the customer isolation fence could be bypassed. More directly: user-controlled keys injected into `qvars` from `parsed_vars` could collide with and overwrite security-critical bind variables (`customers`, `from_date`, `to_date`, etc.) that enforce multi-tenant access control, depending on the order of insertion and how psycopg2 resolves duplicate keys. In the base code this was impossible because `qvars` was always `dict()` at that point; the PR newly introduces the risk by seeding `qvars` with attacker-controlled content before the authorization filters are merged in.

Custom backends example
=======================

Provided example consists of a database backend based on standard PostgreSQL backend.

It has a very basic functionality, adding an attribute to the alert before storing it
in the database. This functionality can be achieved using plugins, it is just an example.

Custom backends must provide a class named 'Backend' that implements `alerta.database.base.Backend`.

The module providing that class must be referenced as an 'alerta.database.backends' entry-point in
python package setup.

```
   ...
    entry_points={
        'alerta.database.backends': [
            'custom = package'
        ]
    }
    ...
```

To use the custom database backend, the name used for the entry-point has to be used as schema in
`DATABASE_URL` configuration setting:

```
DATABASE_URL = "custom://user@db_server/monitoring?connect_timeout=10&application_name=alerta"
```

Custom backends example
=======================

Provided example consists of a database backend based on standard PostgreSQL backend.

It has a very basic functionality, adding an attribute to the alert before storing it
in the database. This functionality can be achieved using plugins, it is just an example.

Custom backends must provide a class named 'Backend' that implements `alerta.database.base.Backend`.

The module providing that class must be referenced as an 'alerta.database.backends' entry-point in
python package setup.

```
   ...
    entry_points={
        'alerta.database.backends': [
            'custom = package'
        ]
    }
    ...
```

To use the custom database backend, the name used for the entry-point has to be used as schema in
`DATABASE_URL` configuration setting:

```
DATABASE_URL = "custom://user@db_server/monitoring?connect_timeout=10&application_name=alerta"
```

The module providing that class must be referenced as an 'alerta.database.backends' entry-point in
python package setup.

```
   ...
    entry_points={
        'alerta.database.backends': [
            'custom = package'
        ]
    }
    ...

To use the custom database backend, the name used for the entry-point has to be used as schema in
`DATABASE_URL` configuration setting:

```
DATABASE_URL = "custom://user@db_server/monitoring?connect_timeout=10&application_name=alerta"
